You can add in terms but it rarely follows and lists them well.  Think of this app and Indeed in general as being like Amazon:  it will find you things, 99% which do not match your search criteria.  

Ask to search for jobs in a specific town or province, yes you might get some, but more likely you will get a lot which are out of your country, state or province and definitely outside your city.  You could almost swear the people who wrote the search algorithms got paid by the number of item they returned instead of accurate item percentages (which for a job seeker that should be close to 100%, but alas with this app it’s closer to 5-10% and strangely enough the more specific you are, the less accurate the results are, so instead of returning just 2 or 3 results that match 100%, you often get dozens, even hundreds of results with an average accuracy of 4% — not good).  And this replaced Monster which had a much higher accuracy?

Good points: there are lots of jobs. Bad points: I applied to a company, got an offer from a company that had rejected me, and then got a second rejection email. I don't remember applying anywhere, so getting two rejections is annoying. Many listings contradict the stated age limit (for example 'up to age 35 for career development' while people in their 50s are working there). I want to be able to hide jobs by age. If that's not possible, then if they are recruiting under the career development framing, they should write it in the first line of the requirements. Addendum: on the smartphone app only, it's hard to view company reviews. Tapping 'company name ★☆☆☆☆ 1.0' shows nothing, and the company info tab doesn't show them either. If there are reviews from people who got hired, there should also be reviews from interviewees. Even if you write honestly, a system where reviews get withdrawn is pointless, because if the honest reviews are taken down, others can't use them as reference. Companies posting here generally look down on job seekers, so this should be thought of as the last bastion of job hunting. When a company has you apply here but then sends you to an external site to apply, is that for collecting personal information?

Before Indeed added their AI elements, this site and subsequent app were much more user friendly. 
The current version has a useless smart search function. It never remembers your preset preferences and the suggested job listings it pulls based on the resume upload are wildly unrelated to actual career experience.(Example: the app will not stop showing me construction and IT jobs as high match jobs even though I have zero experience in either and have maxed out my preferences to omit all the types of construction and IT positions that keep turning up in results.)  
Nor does it even follow the simple search prompt for maintaining a specific salary or location baseline consistently. 
The AI “scout” freezes then crashes the app more often than not. It also turns up the same job listings I responded to with the thumbs down feedback from the search tab. Indeed appears to not have integrated their scout with the regular search option as every time you open the app, you are back at square one. 
On the positive side, I have received real job interviews from Indeed applications vs all the scams and inexperienced recruiter experiences that I’ve dealt with on LinkedIn. 
Indeed also takes security and non-AI related bug reports seriously in a timely manner. Ideally, I’d like to see this company dump the AI assistant and shore up their search functions again.

A Great Resource for Finding Employment Opportunities

Indeed has been one of the most helpful resources I’ve used during my job search. I appreciate how easy it is to search for positions based on location, experience, salary, and job type. hold employers & recruiters to a much higher standard.

Indeed needs to hold employers and recruiters to a much higher standard.

If an employer posts a job and actively solicits applications, candidates should not be left completely ignored afterward. Applicants spend time tailoring resumes, answering screening questions, and submitting information because they reasonably believe the position is actually being recruited for.

Indeed should do more to discourage employers from posting positions that are inactive, already filled, or effectively abandoned. At minimum, candidates deserve acknowledgment that their application was received and, ideally, a basic status update.

Job seekers are people, not database entries. If employers are allowed to use Indeed to recruit, there should be a greater expectation that they communicate with the candidates who apply.

Indeed is easy to use, but don’t count on it for getting a job. Most employers throw their listings on there nowadays and either forget to take them off after hiring someone or use AI to screen applications and automatically throw out a bunch of resumes. Many will not update you on your status as a candidate as well. I appreciate Indeed’s messaging feature, but most of the time, employers will not read or reply to messages. Indeed makes it easy to apply to jobs, but the company needs to do a much better job at holding employers accountable. There should be limits to how long a job listing can stay up, responses to applicants should be required, and employer use of AI to screen applicants must also be regulated. I recommend applying directly through employer websites or going in person to inquire about positions that are open. I am disappointed in Indeed’s performance as a site that is supposed to benefit applicants just as much as it does employers.

A Broken Ad-Delivery Trap Masquerading as a Job Board

Do not waste your phone’s storage or your mental sanity on this app. Indeed is no longer a job search engine; it is a broken corporate ad network that actively penalizes highly skilled job seekers to force-feed paid advertisements down your throat.The platform's underlying technology and mobile search engine are completely defective. I set up a localized custom search string that your automated system proudly boasted had matched 7,349 new jobs. But the moment you click the live notification, the engine panics, cracks under the weight of its own code, and collapses the live results page down to exactly 15 jobs.Even worse, the app completely ignores basic search commands. I utilized standard text filters to explicitly exclude massive local industries I am completely unqualified for or have no interest in (such as -title:CDL, -title:RN, -title:Driver). What did Indeed’s algorithm do? It completely ignored the negative commands and insulted my intelligence by filling my screen with high-priority sponsored ads for "Mental Health Technicians" and "Sale Day Drivers."When you try to use advanced positive grouping logic to look for specialized creative fields (like media, video, audio, or non-profit roles), the mobile app completely strips out your formatting commands. It turns your search query into a random word-soup, stops tracking text titles entirely, and defaults to dumping a lazy, generic list of irrelevant corporate ads based purely on your phone’s GPS location data. I expanded my search radius to include the entire Nashville metropolitan area a massive global media, music, and non-profit hub and this app spat back a grand total of 5 results. It is mathematically impossible for a market of that size to only have 5 creative openings.Here is the truth of what Indeed is doing: They have abandoned the organic job seeker. They have wiped out thousands of authentic, small-scale local postings by forcing employers behind an aggressive paywall. They are financially incentivized to hide real, relevant jobs from you so they can force deep-pocketed corporate ads onto your screen. They are betting on your economic desperation to keep you clicking through a glitchy, user-hostile interface while they charge employers premium prices for dwindling results.This app functions like a casino designed to steal your time, scrape your professional data, and protect its paid corporate advertisers at the absolute expense of your user experience. I am permanently deleting my account, removing the app, and taking my job search to platforms that actually respect basic text queries. Avoid this platform at all costs.

This service I will preface by saying has had its uses over the course of my working life. But its uses were isolated to what I would call low skill jobs. Now that the work search has increased in value, there is 100 fold the amount of scam embedded within indeed. And I will say scam through users trying to take advantage of would be job seekers. I personally would advocate that indeed needs to reevaluate its employer vetting. When you legitimately have to be concerned, if the employer you’re talking to, is trying to steal your identity and if it’s legitimate at all, is a problem. And this problem affects both customers i.e. employers and would be applicants. Employers are harmed because any quality candidates will probably pick up on the same trend and also no longer use the service or others like it. It hurts its would be applicants by hiding potential jobs in the fuzz. Not only indeed, but almost every other service like this is plagued with the same low integrity individuals / scam corps. I would definitely reconfigure how employers validate and verify their own integrity before luring would be applicants. Let’s make this a viable service and not just another example as to why and balances are important and how they affect negatively on standing companies. Thank you

I’ve been using indeed for a a few years now with a few minor annoyances, however with recent AI and UI changes, I’ve had problems. Most of the issues are systemic, such as not having employers post an estimated pay range, have inaccurate locations posted on job listings, and not holding employers accountable for ghosting applicants. All of that can be argued is not part of Indeed’s job. 

However, what can’t be argued is the fact that somewhere in the last six months, indeed’s software simply ate half of my resume. Random portions are gone that were there before, and the only reason I know is because it notified me on the app this morning when I opened it. l’ve applied for countless jobs in the last few months, and the fact that I’ve sent a half completed resume (that was fully completed before) is mortifying. I don’t know how many potential higher paying positions this has cost me, and the more I think about it, the more irritated I get. Why would employers bother to get back to me if it looks like I can’t be bothered to send them a completed resume? 

I shouldn’t have to check to see if the most basic feature of a job search app is working every time I submit an application, but now it seems that I am going to have to. The point of the app is to make searching and applying for jobs easier and less stressful, and it has failed on every front. If I could give negative stars, I would.

Search has not been working properly for many years. It is very hard to use. When I enter words such as employment type, job content, work location, or work hours, a very large number of jobs unrelated to those words appear, while jobs that match the words are few. Also, jobs that are still posted (not marked as ended) often do not appear in search results even when I enter the company name. Results also show over 1000 hits, but only about 20 actually appear. For example, I specified a city, set employment type to dispatch, and searched for driver: 400 results. However, of the 25 jobs on the first page, only 2 were dispatch. Page 2 had 7, page 3 had 5, page 4 had 2. Only 16 of the 100 matched the specified conditions. There were also some duplicate jobs. In conclusion, for many years I have had the impression that search goes well beyond the level of sometimes being slightly off.

I really dislike the new job-filtering/recommendation feature.

I really dislike the new job-filtering/recommendation feature. Indeed seems to be deciding which jobs it thinks I should see instead of simply letting me search the job market myself.

I use different resumes for different purposes, so one profile or resume cannot accurately determine every job I may want to apply for. I have literally seen jobs while logged out that fit my qualifications, but those same jobs don’t appear when I’m logged in.

This is a problem because it can:

• Hide opportunities I may qualify for
• Prevent me from exploring different career paths
• Make assumptions about what jobs I want
• Penalize people who use multiple resumes for different industries
• Give users less control over their own job search
• Make the job market appear smaller than it actually is
• Force users to rely on an algorithm instead of letting them decide for themselves

Recommendations are fine as an optional feature, but they should NOT determine what jobs a user is allowed to see.

Please give users an option to turn personalized filtering OFF and view a more complete, unfiltered list of search results.

Let the job seeker decide what they want to apply for.
